newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reform group urges Friday strike and marches.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reform group urges Friday strike and marches.

text.p: An alliance of opposition-backed groups called on Tuesday for a general strike and protest marches in Kenya on Friday, and a go-slow of air traffic controllers caused travel havoc for a fourth day.
The National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), grouping opposition, church and civic groups, urged Kenyans to join marches on Friday, raising the spectre of violent clashes with riot police.

"The NCEC calls upon business owners, shopkeepers, transport operators and all citizens to stop work on August 8 throughout the country. We appeal to all Kenyans to join in the proposed peaceful processions," the alliance said in a statement.

The opposition party FORD-Kenya, whose leader Michael Wamalwa met President Daniel arap Moi for talks last month, urged the NCEC to call off the strike, arguing political parties alone should conduct political action.

The NCEC refused to apply for official licences for a series of rallies in June and July to press for constitutional reforms, leading to violent clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators that rattled foreign investors and tourists.
But Moi's government blunted a rally called by the NCEC in the Indian Ocean city of Mombasa on July 26 by licensing it although organisers never applied for a permit.
Moi, 73 and in power since 1978, and the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party are still widely expected to win a general election that must be held later this year.
The general strike is aimed at keeping up the pressure on Moi in the wake of the International Monetary Fund last Thursday halting a key aid package for Kenya because of corruption.

On the fourth day of a go-slow by air traffic controllers in Kenya, airlines cancelled, diverted or rescheduled flights on Tuesday. National carrier Kenya Airways said it had to cancel six flights on Tuesday and Wednesday and reschedule others.
The controllers say they are paid about $90 a month and are demanding a 50-fold pay increase and improved benefits.
Aviation officials said talks collapsed on Monday when the air controllers rejected a government request to return to work and give Kenyan authorities two weeks to study their demands.
"The situation might get worse unless some agreement is reached. At the moment there are three-hour delays, but they could delay things for six hours," said an airport official.
The NCEC urged the controllers to escalate their go-slow to a strike.
The government on Monday called for investor calm and said Kenyans should become self-reliant after the IMF decision.
But business and opposition leaders rejected the government statement as nonsense and argued that corruption, not the IMF decision, was at the root of Kenya's economic difficulties.
The Kenyan shilling suffered further losses after a shortfall in expected dollar inflows from agricultural exporters, commercial dealers said on Tuesday.
Foreign exchange dealers said the shilling slid to close at 63.60/64.90 on Tuesday mid-afternoon after holding stable for most of the day at 62.50/63.50 -- a 2.2 percent drop.
Commercial bank dealers said the central bank sold up to $21 million to meet orders from foreign investors who wanted to sell government treasury bills because of the IMF move.
The shilling was unchanged from Monday's close but it has fallen a total of 6.72 percent since Thursday's close.

The Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) share index fell on Tuesday for the third successive day since the IMF cancelled its aid package. The 20-share index fell 19.47 points to 3408.75 from 3428.22 at Monday's close. The index tumbled 24.95 points on Monday.
